To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) ctDNA concentration in plasma increases with tumor growth, (2) ctDNA is mostly composed of mononucleosomes, and (3) ctDNA is mainly of tumor origin.
the concentration of human ctDNA increased significantly during CRC tumor growth, whereas the level of mouse ctDNAs remained constant.

(1) we developed an in vivo model to study ctDNA release and fragmentation in mice with colorectal carcinoma; (2) we demonstrated that the concentration of ctDNA in plasma increases significantly with tumor growth and that ctDNA fragmentation is more pronounced for bigger tumors; (3) we confirmed that apoptosis is the main source of ctDNA in CRC; (4) we showed that ctDNA features differ between patients with advanced disease and healthy individuals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new experimental system for the study of ctDNA in CRC and the analysis of the origin and quantification of this DNA in mice with CRC xenografts.
the development of a new experimental model to investigate the origin of ctDNA and its potential clinical use in CRC.

the development of a new experimental system to investigate circulating DNA in mice bearing human colorectal cancer cells xenografts, which might be useful to study the role of ctDNA in cancer development and progression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the amount of ctDNA increases with tumor size, but that the origin of the circulating DNA is not only apoptotic but also necrotic.
, although the origin of circulating DNA is still debated, it is likely to be a combination of apoptosis, necrosis, and shedding from the cell surface.
the ctDNA features in the plasma from CRC patients and CRC xenografted animals are different.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the amount of circulating ctDNA increases during tumor development and the fragmentation pattern of tumor ctDNA is different in mice with smaller or larger tumors.
ctDNA is released from tumor cells in a size and concentration-dependent manner and that the rate of release is related to the rate of tumor growth.
the origin and quantification of ctDNA in xenografted mice with human colorectum cancer is a good model to understand the biology of this biomarker.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the concentration of tumor-derived ctDNA increases with tumor growth, while mouse ctDNA remains constant.
, by using the described model system, we could discriminate ctDNA derived from tumor cells from that of normal cells.
the origin, form and release rate of ctDNA are not fixed but vary with tumor growth and, as a result, the interpretation of the clinical significance of ctDNA should be carefully considered.
